passages.text: ***SCENE:** The Athenian Ecclesia on the Pnyx; afterwards Dicæopolis' house in the country.*
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS**[1] (*alone*) What cares have not gnawed at my heart and how few have been the pleasures in my life! Four, to be exact, while my troubles have been as countless as the grains of sand on the shore! Let me see of what value to me have been these few pleasures? Ah! I remember that I was delighted in soul when Cleon had to disgorge those five talents;[2] I was in ecstasy and I love the Knights for this deed; 'it is an honour to Greece.'[3] But the day when I was impatiently awaiting a piece by Æschylus,[4] what tragic despair it caused me when the herald called, "Theognis,[5] introduce your Chorus!" Just imagine how this blow struck straight at my heart! On the other hand, what joy Dexitheus caused me at the musical competition, when he played a Bœotian melody on the lyre! But this year by contrast! Oh! what deadly torture to hear Chæris[6] perform the prelude in the Orthian mode![7]—Never, however, since I began to bathe, has the dust hurt my eyes as it does to-day. Still it is the day of assembly; all should be here at daybreak, and yet the Pnyx[8] is still deserted. They are gossiping in the market-place, slipping hither and thither to avoid the vermilioned rope.[9] The Prytanes[10] even do not come; they will be late, but when they come they will push and fight each other for a seat in the front row. They will never trouble themselves with the question of peace. Oh! Athens! Athens! As for myself, I do not fail to come here before all the rest, and now, finding myself alone, I groan, yawn, stretch, break wind, and know not what to do; I make sketches in the dust, pull out my loose hairs, muse, think of my fields, long for peace, curse town life and regret my dear country home,[11] which never told me to 'buy fuel, vinegar or oil'; there the word 'buy,' which cuts me in two, was unknown; I harvested everything at will. Therefore I have come to the assembly fully prepared to bawl, interrupt and abuse the speakers, if they talk of aught but peace. But here come the Prytanes, and high time too, for it is midday! As I foretold, hah! is it not so? They are pushing and fighting for the front seats.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Move on up, move on, move on, to get within the consecrated area.[12]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** Has anyone spoken yet?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Who asks to speak?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** You are no man.[13]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** No! I am an immortal! Amphitheus was the son of Ceres and Triptolemus; of him was born Celeus. Celeus wedded Phæncreté, my grandmother, whose son was Lucinus, and, being born of him, I am an immortal; it is to me alone that the gods have entrusted the duty of treating with the Lacedæmonians. But, citizens, though I am immortal, I am dying of hunger; the Prytanes give me naught.[14]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** Oh, Triptolemus and Ceres, do ye thus forsake your own blood?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Prytanes, in expelling this citizen, you are offering an outrage to the Assembly. He only desired to secure peace for us and to sheathe the sword.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **PRYTANIS** Sit down and keep silence!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, by Apollo, will I not, unless you are going to discuss the question of peace.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** The ambassadors, who are returned from the Court of the King!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Of what King? I am sick of all those fine birds, the peacock ambassadors and their swagger.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! oh! by Ecbatana,[15] what assumption!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AN AMBASSADOR** During the archonship of Euthymenes, you sent us to the Great King on a salary of two drachmæ per diem.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! those poor drachmæ!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** We suffered horribly on the plains of the Caÿster, sleeping under a tent, stretched deliciously on fine chariots, half dead with weariness.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And I was very much at ease, lying on the straw along the battlements![16]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** Everywhere we were well received and forced to drink delicious wine out of golden or crystal flagons….
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh, city of Cranaus,[17] thy ambassadors are laughing at thee!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** For great feeders and heavy drinkers are alone esteemed as men by the barbarians.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Just as here in Athens, we only esteem the most drunken debauchees.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** At the end of the fourth year we reached the King's Court, but he had left with his whole army to ease himself, and for the space of eight months he was thus easing himself in midst of the golden mountains.[18]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And how long was he replacing his dress?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** The whole period of a full moon; after which he returned to his palace; then he entertained us and had us served with oxen roasted whole in an oven.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Who ever saw an oxen baked in an oven? What a lie!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** On my honour, he also had us served with a bird three times as large as Cleonymus,[19] and called the Boaster.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And do we give you two drachmæ, that you should treat us to all this humbug?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** We are bringing to you, Pseudartabas,[20] the King's Eye.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I would a crow might pluck out thine with his beak, thou cursed ambassador!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Eh! Great gods! Friend, with thy great eye, round like the hole through which the oarsman passes his sweep, you have the air of a galley doubling a cape to gain the port.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** Come, Pseudartabas, give forth the message for the Athenians with which you were charged by the Great King.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **PSEUDARTABAS** Jartaman exarx 'anapissonnai satra.[21]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** Do you understand what he says?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** By Apollo, not I!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** He says, that the Great King will send you gold. Come, utter the word 'gold' louder and more distinctly.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Thou shalt not have gold, thou gaping-arsed Ionian.[22]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! may the gods forgive me, but that is clear enough.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** What does he say?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** That the Ionians are debauchees and idiots, if they expect to receive gold from the barbarians.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMBASSADOR** Not so, he speaks of medimni[23] of gold.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What medimni? Thou art but a great braggart; but get your way, I will find out the truth by myself. Come now, answer me clearly, if you do not wish me to dye your skin red. Will the Great King send us gold? (*Pseudartabas makes a negative sign.*) Then our ambassadors are seeking to deceive us? (*Pseudartabas signs affirmatively.*) These fellows make signs like any Greek; I am sure that they are nothing but Athenians. Oh, ho! I recognize one of these eunuchs; it is Clisthenes, the son of Sibyrtius.[24] Behold the effrontery of this shaven rump! How! great baboon, with such a beard do you seek to play the eunuch to us? And this other one? Is it not Straton?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Silence! Let all be seated. The Senate invites the King's Eye to the Prytaneum.[25]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Is this not sufficient to drive one to hang oneself? Here I stand chilled to the bone, whilst the doors of the Prytaneum fly wide open to lodge such rascals. But I will do something great and bold. Where is Amphitheus? Come and speak with me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Take these eight drachmæ and go and conclude a truce with the Lacedæmonians for me, my wife and my children; I leave you free, my dear citizens, to send out embassies and to stand gaping in the air.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Bring in Theorus, who has returned from the Court of Sitalces.[26]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Another humbug!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **THEORUS** We should not have remained long in Thrace….
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Forsooth, no, if you had not been well paid.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **THEORUS** … If the country had not been covered with snow; the rivers were ice-bound at the time that Theognis[27] brought out his tragedy here; during the whole of that time I was holding my own with Sitalces, cup in hand; and, in truth, he adored you to such a degree, that he wrote on the walls, "How beautiful are the Athenians!" His son, to whom we gave the freedom of the city, burned with desire to come here and eat chitterlings at the feast of the Apaturia;[28] he prayed his father to come to the aid of his new country and Sitalces swore on his goblet that he would succour us with such a host that the Athenians would exclaim, "What a cloud of grasshoppers!"
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** May I die if I believe a word of what you tell us! Excepting the grasshoppers, there is not a grain of truth in it all!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **THEORUS** And he has sent you the most warlike soldiers of all Thrace.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Now we shall begin to see clearly.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Come hither, Thracians, whom Theorus brought.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What plague have we here?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **THEORUS** 'Tis the host of the Odomanti.[29]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Of the Odomanti? Tell me what it means. Who has mutilated their tools like this?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **THEORUS** If they are given a wage of two drachmæ, they will put all Bœotia[30] to fire and sword.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Two drachmæ to those circumcised hounds! Groan aloud, ye people of rowers, bulwark of Athens! Ah! great gods! I am undone; these Odomanti are robbing me of my garlic![31] Will you give me back my garlic?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **THEORUS** Oh! wretched man! do not go near them; they have eaten garlic.[32]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Prytanes, will you let me be treated in this manner, in my own country and by barbarians? But I oppose the discussion of paying a wage to the Thracians; I announce an omen; I have just felt a drop of rain.[33]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Let the Thracians withdraw and return the day after to-morrow; the Prytanes declare the sitting at an end.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ye gods, what garlic I have lost! But here comes Amphitheus returned from Lacedæmon. Welcome, Amphitheus.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** No, there is no welcome for me and I fly as fast as I can, for I am pursued by the Acharnians.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Why, what has happened?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** I was hurrying to bring your treaty of truce, but some old dotards from Acharnæ[34] got scent of the thing; they are veterans of Marathon, tough as oak or maple, of which they are made for sure—rough and ruthless. They all set to a-crying, "Wretch! you are the bearer of a treaty, and the enemy has only just cut our vines!" Meanwhile they were gathering stones in their cloaks, so I fled and they ran after me shouting.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Let 'em shout as much as they please! But have you brought me a treaty?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** Most certainly, here are three samples to select from,[35] this one is five years old; take it and taste.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** It does not please me; it smells of pitch and of the ships they are fitting out.[36]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** Here is another, ten years old; taste it.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** It smells strongly of the delegates, who go round the towns to chide the allies for their slowness.[37]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** This last is a truce of thirty years, both on sea and land.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! by Bacchus! what a bouquet! It has the aroma of nectar and ambrosia; this does not say to us, "Provision yourselves for three days." But it lisps the gentle numbers, "Go whither you will."[38] I accept it, ratify it, drink it at one draught and consign the Acharnians to limbo. Freed from the war and its ills, I shall keep the Dionysia[39] in the country.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AMPHITHEUS** And I shall run away, for I'm mortally afraid of the Acharnians.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** This way all! Let us follow our man; we will demand him of everyone we meet; the public weal makes his seizure imperative. Ho, there! tell me which way the bearer of the truce has gone; he has escaped us, he has disappeared. Curse old age! When I was young, in the days when I followed Phayllus,[40] running with a sack of coals on my back, this wretch would not have eluded my pursuit, let him be as swift as he will; but now my limbs are stiff; old Lacratides[41] feels his legs are weighty and the traitor escapes me. No, no, let us follow him; old Acharnians like ourselves shall not be set at naught by a scoundrel, who has dared, great gods! to conclude a truce, when I wanted the war continued with double fury in order to avenge my ruined lands. No mercy for our foes until I have pierced their hearts like a sharp reed, so that they dare never again ravage my vineyards. Come, let us seek the rascal; let us look everywhere, carrying our stones in our hands; let us hunt him from place to place until we trap him; I could never, never tire of the delight of stoning him.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Peace! profane men![42]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Silence all! Friends, do you hear the sacred formula? Here is he, whom we seek! This way, all! Get out of his way, surely he comes to offer an oblation.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Peace, profane men! Let the basket-bearer[43] come forward, and thou, Xanthias, hold the phallus well upright.[44]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **WIFE OF DICÆOPOLIS** Daughter, set down the basket and let us begin the sacrifice.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DAUGHTER OF DICÆOPOLIS** Mother, hand me the ladle, that I may spread the sauce on the cake.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** It is well! Oh, mighty Bacchus, it is with joy that, freed from military duty, I and all mine perform this solemn rite and offer thee this sacrifice; grant, that I may keep the rural Dionysia without hindrance and that this truce of thirty years may be propitious for me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **WIFE OF DICÆOPOLIS** Come, my child, carry the basket gracefully and with a grave, demure face. Happy he, who shall be your possessor and embrace you so firmly at dawn,[45] that you belch wind like a weasel. Go forward, and have a care they don't snatch your jewels in the crowd.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Xanthias, walk behind the basket-bearer and hold the phallus well erect; I will follow, singing the Phallic hymn; thou, wife, look on from the top of the terrace.[46] Forward! Oh, Phales,[47] companion of the orgies of Bacchus, night reveller, god of adultery, friend of young men, these past six[48] years I have not been able to invoke thee. With what joy I return to my farmstead, thanks to the truce I have concluded, freed from cares, from fighting and from Lamachuses![49] How much sweeter, Phales, oh, Phales, is it to surprise Thratta, the pretty wood-maid, Strymodorus' slave, stealing wood from Mount Phelleus, to catch her under the arms, to throw her on the ground and possess her! Oh, Phales, Phales! If thou wilt drink and bemuse thyself with me, we will to-morrow consume some good dish in honour of the peace, and I will hang up my buckler over the smoking hearth.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** It is he, he himself. Stone him, stone him, stone him, strike the wretch. All, all of you, pelt him, pelt him!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What is this? By Heracles, you will smash my pot.[50]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** It is you that we are stoning, you miserable scoundrel.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And for what sin, Acharnian Elders, tell me that!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** You ask that, you impudent rascal, traitor to your country; you alone amongst us all have concluded a truce, and you dare to look us in the face!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But you do not know why I have treated for peace. Listen!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Listen to you? No, no, you are about to die, we will annihilate you with our stones.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But first of all, listen. Stop, my friends.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** I will hear nothing; do not address me; I hate you more than I do Cleon,[51] whom one day I shall flay to make sandals for the Knights. Listen to your long speeches, after you have treated with the Laconians! No, I will punish you.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Friends, leave the Laconians out of debate and consider only whether I have not done well to conclude my truce.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Done well! when you have treated with a people who know neither gods, nor truth, nor faith.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** We attribute too much to the Laconians; as for myself, I know that they are not the cause of all our troubles.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Oh, indeed, rascal! You dare to use such language to me and then expect me to spare you!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, no, they are not the cause of all our troubles, and I who address you claim to be able to prove that they have much to complain of in us.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** This passes endurance; my heart bounds with fury. Thus you dare to defend our enemies.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Were my head on the block I would uphold what I say and rely on the approval of the people.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Comrades, let us hurl our stones and dye this fellow purple.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What black fire-brand has inflamed your heart! You will not hear me? You really will not, Acharnians?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** No, a thousand times, no.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** This is a hateful injustice.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** May I die, if I listen.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Nay, nay! have mercy, have mercy, Acharnians.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Well, blood for blood! I will kill your dearest friend. I have here the hostages of Acharnæ;[52] I shall disembowel them.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Acharnians, what means this threat? Has he got one of our children in his house? What gives him such audacity?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Stone me, if it please you; I shall avenge myself on this. (*Shows a basket.*) Let us see whether you have any love for your coals.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Great gods! this basket is our fellow-citizen. Stop, stop, in heaven's name!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I shall dismember it despite your cries; I will listen to nothing.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** How! will you kill this coal-basket, my beloved comrade?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Just now, you did not listen to me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Well, speak now, if you will; tell us, tell us you have a weakness for the Lacedæmonians. I consent to anything; never will I forsake this dear little basket.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** First, throw down your stones.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** There! 'tis done. And you, do you put away your sword.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Let me see that no stones remain concealed in your cloaks.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** They are all on the ground; see how we shake our garments. Come, no haggling, lay down your sword; we threw away everything while crossing from one side of the stage to the other.[53]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What cries of anguish you would have uttered had these coals of Parnes[54] been dismembered, and yet it came very near it; had they perished, their death would have been due to the folly of their fellow-citizens. The poor basket was so frightened, look, it has shed a thick black dust over me, the same as a cuttle-fish does. What an irritable temper! You shout and throw stones, you will not hear my arguments—not even when I propose to speak in favour of the Lacedæmonians with my head on the block; and yet I cling to my life.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Well then, bring out a block before your door, scoundrel, and let us hear the good grounds you can give us; I am curious to know them. Now mind, as you proposed yourself, place your head on the block and speak.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Here is the block; and, though I am but a very sorry speaker, I wish nevertheless to talk freely of the Lacedæmonians and without the protection of my buckler. Yet I have many reasons for fear. I know our rustics; they are delighted if some braggart comes, and rightly or wrongly loads both them and their city with praise and flattery; they do not see that such toad-eaters[55] are traitors, who sell them for gain. As for the old men, I know their weakness; they only seek to overwhelm the accused with their votes.[56] Nor have I forgotten how Cleon treated me because of my comedy last year;[57] he dragged me before the Senate and there he uttered endless slanders against me; 'twas a tempest of abuse, a deluge of lies. Through what a slough of mud he dragged me! I nigh perished. Permit me, therefore, before I speak, to dress in the manner most likely to draw pity.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** What evasions, subterfuges and delays! Hold! here is the sombre helmet of Pluto with its thick bristling plume; Hieronymus[58] lends it to you; then open Sisyphus'[59] bag of wiles; but hurry, hurry, pray, for our discussion does not admit of delay.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** The time has come for me to manifest my courage, so I will go and seek Euripides. Ho! slave, slave!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Is Euripides at home?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SLAVE** He is and he isn't; understand that, if you have wit for't.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** How? He is and he isn't![60]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SLAVE** Certainly, old man; busy gathering subtle fancies here and there, his mind is not in the house, but he himself is; perched aloft, he is composing a tragedy.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh, Euripides, you are indeed happy to have a slave so quick at repartee! Now, fellow, call your master.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** So much the worse. But I will not go. Come, let us knock at the door. Euripides, my little Euripides, my darling Euripides, listen; never had man greater right to your pity. It is Dicæopolis of the Chollidan Deme who calls you. Do you hear?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** I have no time to waste.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Very well, have yourself wheeled out here.[61]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Nevertheless….
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Well, let them roll me out; as to coming down, I have not the time.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** What words strike my ear?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** You perch aloft to compose tragedies, when you might just as well do them on the ground. I am not astonished at your introducing cripples on the stage.[62] And why dress in these miserable tragic rags? I do not wonder that your heroes are beggars. But, Euripides, on my knees I beseech you, give me the tatters of some old piece: for I have to treat the Chorus to a long speech, and if I do it ill it is all over with me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** What rags do you prefer? Those in which I rigged out Æneus[63] on the stage, that unhappy, miserable old man?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, I want those of some hero still more unfortunate.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Of Phœnix, the blind man?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, not of Phœnix, you have another hero more unfortunate than him.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Now, what tatters does he want? Do you mean those of the beggar Philoctetes?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, of another far more the mendicant.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Is it the filthy dress of the lame fellow, Bellerophon?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, 'tis not Bellerophon; he, whom I mean, was not only lame and a beggar, but boastful and a fine speaker.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Ah! I know, it is Telephus, the Mysian.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Yes, Telephus. Give me his rags, I beg of you.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Slave! give him Telephus' tatters; they are on top of the rags of Thyestes and mixed with those of Ino.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SLAVE** Catch hold! here they are.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! Zeus, whose eye pierces everywhere and embraces all, permit me to assume the most wretched dress on earth. Euripides, cap your kindness by giving me the little Mysian hat, that goes so well with these tatters. I must to-day have the look of a beggar; "be what I am, but not appear to be";[64] the audience will know well who I am, but the Chorus will be fools enough not to, and I shall dupe 'em with my subtle phrases.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** I will give you the hat; I love the clever tricks of an ingenious brain like yours.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Rest happy, and may it befall Telephus as I wish. Ah! I already feel myself filled with quibbles. But I must have a beggar's staff.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Here you are, and now get you gone from this porch.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh, my soul! You see how you are driven from this house, when I still need so many accessories. But let us be pressing, obstinate, importunate. Euripides, give me a little basket with a lamp alight inside.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Whatever do you want such a thing as that for?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I do not need it, but I want it all the same.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** You importune me; get you gone!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Alas! may the gods grant you a destiny as brilliant as your mother's.[65]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Leave me in peace.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! just a little broken cup.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Take it and go and hang yourself. What a tiresome fellow!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! you do not know all the pain you cause me. Dear, good Euripides, nothing beyond a small pipkin stoppered with a sponge.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Miserable man! You are robbing me of an entire tragedy.[66] Here, take it and be off.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I am going, but, great gods! I need one thing more; unless I have it, I am a dead man. Hearken, my little Euripides, only give me this and I go, never to return. For pity's sake, do give me a few small herbs for my basket.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** You wish to ruin me then. Here, take what you want; but it is all over with my pieces!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I won't ask another thing; I'm going. I am too importunate and forget that I rouse against me the hate of kings.—Ah! wretch that I am! I am lost! I have forgotten one thing, without which all the rest is as nothing. Euripides, my excellent Euripides, my dear little Euripides, may I die if I ask you again for the smallest present; only one, the last, absolutely the last; give me some of the chervil your mother left you in her will.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **EURIPIDES** Insolent hound! Slave, lock the door.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh, my soul! I must go away without the chervil. Art thou sensible of the dangerous battle we are about to engage upon in defending the Lacedæmonians? Courage, my soul, we must plunge into the midst of it. Dost thou hesitate and art thou fully steeped in Euripides? That's right! do not falter, my poor heart, and let us risk our head to say what we hold for truth. Courage and boldly to the front. I wonder I am so brave!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** What do you purport doing? what are you going to say? What an impudent fellow! what a brazen heart! To dare to stake his head and uphold an opinion contrary to that of us all! And he does not tremble to face this peril! Come, it is you who desired it, speak!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Spectators, be not angered if, although I am a beggar, I dare in a Comedy to speak before the people of Athens of the public weal; Comedy too can sometimes discern what is right. I shall not please, but I shall say what is true. Besides, Cleon shall not be able to accuse me of attacking Athens before strangers;[67] we are by ourselves at the festival of the Lenæa; the period when our allies send us their tribute and their soldiers is not yet. Here is only the pure wheat without chaff; as to the resident strangers settled among us, they and the citizens are one, like the straw and the ear.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: I detest the Lacedæmonians with all my heart, and may Posidon, the god of Tænarus,[68] cause an earthquake and overturn their dwellings! My vines also have been cut. But come (there are only friends who hear me), why accuse the Laconians of all our woes? Some men (I do not say the city, note particularly, that I do not say the city), some wretches, lost in vices, bereft of honour, who were not even citizens of good stamp, but strangers, have accused the Megarians of introducing their produce fraudulently, and not a cucumber, a leveret, a sucking-pig, a clove of garlic, a lump of salt was seen without its being said, "Halloa! these come from Megara," and their being instantly confiscated. Thus far the evil was not serious, and we were the only sufferers. But now some young drunkards go to Megara and carry off the courtesan Simætha; the Megarians, hurt to the quick, run off in turn with two harlots of the house of Aspasia; and so for three gay women Greece is set ablaze. Then Pericles, aflame with ire on his Olympian height, let loose the lightning, caused the thunder to roll, upset Greece and passed an edict, which ran like the song, "That the Megarians be banished both from our land and from our markets and from the sea and from the continent."[69] Meanwhile the Megarians, who were beginning to die of hunger, begged the Lacedæmonians to bring about the abolition of the decree, of which those harlots were the cause; several times we refused their demand; and from that time there was a horrible clatter of arms everywhere. You will say that Sparta was wrong, but what should she have done? Answer that. Suppose that a Lacedæmonian had seized a little Seriphian[70] dog on any pretext and had sold it, would you have endured it quietly? Far from it, you would at once have sent three hundred vessels to sea, and what an uproar there would have been through all the city! there 'tis a band of noisy soldiery, here a brawl about the election of a Trierarch; elsewhere pay is being distributed, the Pallas figure-heads are being regilded, crowds are surging under the market porticos, encumbered with wheat that is being measured, wine-skins, oar-leathers, garlic, olives, onions in nets; everywhere are chaplets, sprats, flute-girls, black eyes; in the arsenal bolts are being noisily driven home, sweeps are being made and fitted with leathers; we hear nothing but the sound of whistles, of flutes and fifes to encourage the work-folk. That is what you assuredly would have done, and would not Telephus have done the same? So I come to my general conclusion; we have no common sense.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **FIRST SEMI-CHORUS** Oh! wretch! oh! infamous man! You are naught but a beggar and yet you dare to talk to us like this! you insult their worships the informers!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SECOND SEMI-CHORUS** By Posidon! he speaks the truth; he has not lied in a single detail.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **FIRST SEMI-CHORUS** But though it be true, need he say it? But you'll have no great cause to be proud of your insolence!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SECOND SEMI-CHORUS** Where are you running to? Don't you move; if you strike this man I shall be at you.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **FIRST SEMI-CHORUS** Lamachus, whose glance flashes lightning, whose plume petrifies thy foes, help! Oh! Lamachus, my friend, the hero of my tribe and all of you, both officers and soldiers, defenders of our walls, come to my aid; else is it all over with me!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Whence comes this cry of battle? where must I bring my aid? where must I sow dread? who wants me to uncase my dreadful Gorgon's head?[71]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh, Lamachus, great hero! Your plumes and your cohorts terrify me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** This man, Lamachus, incessantly abuses Athens.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** You are but a mendicant and you dare to use language of this sort?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh, brave Lamachus, forgive a beggar who speaks at hazard.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** But what have you said? Let us hear.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I know nothing about it; the sight of weapons makes me dizzy. Oh! I adjure you, take that fearful Gorgon somewhat farther away.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Now place it face downwards on the ground.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Give me a plume out of your helmet.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Here is a feather.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And hold my head while I vomit; the plumes have turned my stomach.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Hah! what are you proposing to do? do you want to make yourself vomit with this feather?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Is it a feather? what bird's? a braggart's?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Ah! ah! I will rip you open.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, no, Lamachus! Violence is out of place here! But as you are so strong, why did you not circumcise me? You have all you want for the operation there.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** A beggar dares thus address a general!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** How? Am I a beggar?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** What are you then?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Who am I? A good citizen, not ambitious; a soldier, who has fought well since the outbreak of the war, whereas you are but a vile mercenary.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** They elected me….
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Yes, three cuckoos did![72] If I have concluded peace, 'twas disgust that drove me; for I see men with hoary heads in the ranks and young fellows of your age shirking service. Some are in Thrace getting an allowance of three drachmæ, such fellows as Tisameophœnippus and Panurgipparchides. The others are with Chares or in Chaonia, men like Geretotheodorus and Diomialazon; there are some of the same kidney, too, at Camarina and at Gela,[73] the laughing-stock of all and sundry.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** They were elected.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And why do you always receive your pay, when none of these others ever get any? Speak, Marilades, you have grey hair; well then, have you ever been entrusted with a mission? See! he shakes his head. Yet he is an active as well as a prudent man. And you, Dracyllus, Euphorides or Prinides, have you knowledge of Ecbatana or Chaonia? You say no, do you not? Such offices are good for the son of Cæsyra[74] and Lamachus, who, but yesterday ruined with debt, never pay their shot, and whom all their friends avoid as foot passengers dodge the folks who empty their slops out of window.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! in freedom's name! are such exaggerations to be borne?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Lamachus is well content; no doubt he is well paid, you know.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** But I propose always to war with the Peloponnesians, both at sea, on land and everywhere to make them tremble, and trounce them soundly.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** For my own part, I make proclamation to all Peloponnesians, Megarians and Bœotians, that to them my markets are open; but I debar Lamachus from entering them.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Convinced by this man's speech, the folk have changed their view and approve him for having concluded peace. But let us prepare for the recital of the parabasis.[75]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: Never since our poet presented Comedies, has he praised himself upon the stage; but, having been slandered by his enemies amongst the volatile Athenians, accused of scoffing at his country and of insulting the people, to-day he wishes to reply and regain for himself the inconstant Athenians. He maintains that he has done much that is good for you; if you no longer allow yourselves to be too much hoodwinked by strangers or seduced by flattery, if in politics you are no longer the ninnies you once were, it is thanks to him. Formerly, when delegates from other cities wanted to deceive you, they had but to style you, "the people crowned with violets," and, at the word "violets" you at once sat erect on the tips of your bums. Or, if to tickle your vanity, someone spoke of "rich and sleek Athens," in return for that 'sleekness' he would get all, because he spoke of you as he would have of anchovies in oil. In cautioning you against such wiles, the poet has done you great service as well as in forcing you to understand what is really the democratic principle. Thus, the strangers, who came to pay their tributes, wanted to see this great poet, who had dared to speak the truth to Athens. And so far has the fame of his boldness reached that one day the Great King, when questioning the Lacedæmonian delegates, first asked them which of the two rival cities was the superior at sea, and then immediately demanded at which it was that the comic poet directed his biting satire. "Happy that city," he added, "if it listens to his counsel; it will grow in power, and its victory is assured." This is why the Lacedæmonians offer you peace, if you will cede them Ægina; not that they care for the isle, but they wish to rob you of your poet.[76] As for you, never lose him, who will always fight for the cause of justice in his Comedies; he promises you that his precepts will lead you to happiness, though he uses neither flattery, nor bribery, nor intrigue, nor deceit; instead of loading you with praise, he will point you to the better way. I scoff at Cleon's tricks and plotting; honesty and justice shall fight my cause; never will you find me a political poltroon, a prostitute to the highest bidder.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: I invoke thee, Acharnian Muse, fierce and fell as the devouring fire; sudden as the spark that bursts from the crackling oaken coal when roused by the quickening fan to fry little fishes, while others knead the dough or whip the sharp Thasian pickle with rapid hand, so break forth, my Muse, and inspire thy tribesmen with rough, vigorous, stirring strains.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: We others, now old men and heavy with years, we reproach the city; so many are the victories we have gained for the Athenian fleets that we well deserve to be cared for in our declining life; yet far from this, we are ill-used, harassed with law-suits, delivered over to the scorn of stripling orators. Our minds and bodies being ravaged with age, Posidon should protect us, yet we have no other support than a staff. When standing before the judge, we can scarcely stammer forth the fewest words, and of justice we see but its barest shadow, whereas the accuser, desirous of conciliating the younger men, overwhelms us with his ready rhetoric; he drags us before the judge, presses us with questions, lays traps for us; the onslaught troubles, upsets and rends poor old Tithonus, who, crushed with age, stands tongue-tied; sentenced to a fine,[77] he weeps, he sobs and says to his friend, "This fine robs me of the last trifle that was to have bought my coffin."
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: Is this not a scandal? What! the clepsydra[78] is to kill the white-haired veteran, who, in fierce fighting, has so oft covered himself with glorious sweat, whose valour at Marathon saved the country! 'Twas we who pursued on the field of Marathon, whereas now 'tis wretches who pursue us to the death and crush us! What would Marpsias reply to this?[79] What an injustice, that a man, bent with age like Thucydides, should be brow-beaten by this braggart advocate, Cephisodemus,[80] who is as savage as the Scythian desert he was born in! Is it not to convict him from the outset? I wept tears of pity when I saw an Archer[81] maltreat this old man, who, by Ceres, when he was young and the true Thucydides, would not have permitted an insult from Ceres herself! At that date he would have floored ten miserable orators, he would have terrified three thousand Archers with his shouts; he would have pierced the whole line of the enemy with his shafts. Ah! but if you will not leave the aged in peace, decree that the advocates be matched; thus the old man will only be confronted with a toothless greybeard, the young will fight with the braggart, the ignoble with the son of Clinias[82]; make a law that in future, the old man can only be summoned and convicted at the courts by the aged and the young man by the youth.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** These are the confines of my market-place. All Peloponnesians, Megarians, Bœotians, have the right to come and trade here, provided they sell their wares to me and not to Lamachus. As market-inspectors I appoint these three whips of Leprean[83] leather, chosen by lot. Warned away are all informers and all men of Phasis.[84] They are bringing me the pillar on which the treaty is inscribed[85] and I shall erect it in the centre of the market, well in sight of all.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **A MEGARIAN** Hail! market of Athens, beloved of Megarians. Let Zeus, the patron of friendship, witness, I regretted you as a mother mourns her son. Come, poor little daughters of an unfortunate father, try to find something to eat; listen to me with the full heed of an empty belly. Which would you prefer? To be sold or to cry with hunger.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DAUGHTERS** To be sold, to be sold!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** That is my opinion too. But who would make so sorry a deal as to buy you? Ah! I recall me a Megarian trick; I am going to disguise you as little porkers, that I am offering for sale. Fit your hands with these hoofs and take care to appear the issue of a sow of good breed, for, if I am forced to take you back to the house, by Hermes! you will suffer cruelly of hunger! Then fix on these snouts and cram yourselves into this sack. Forget not to grunt and to say wee-wee like the little pigs that are sacrificed in the Mysteries. I must summon Dicæopolis. Where is he? Dicæopolis, will you buy some nice little porkers?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Who are you? a Megarian?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** I have come to your market.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Well, how are things at Megara?[86]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** We are crying with hunger at our firesides.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** The fireside is jolly enough with a piper. But what else is doing at Megara, eh?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** What else? When I left for the market, the authorities were taking steps to let us die in the quickest manner.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** That is the best way to get you out of all your troubles.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What other news of Megara? What is wheat selling at?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** With us it is valued as highly as the very gods in heaven!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Is it salt that you are bringing?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Are you not holding back the salt?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** 'Tis garlic then?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** What! garlic! do you not at every raid grub up the ground with your pikes to pull out every single head?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What do you bring then?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Little sows, like those they immolate at the Mysteries.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! very well, show me them.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** They are very fine; feel their weight. See! how fat and fine.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But what is this?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** A sow, for a certainty.[87]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** You say a sow! of what country, then?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** From Megara. What! is that not a sow then?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, I don't believe it is.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** This is too much! what an incredulous man! He says 'tis not a sow; but we will stake, an you will, a measure of salt ground up with thyme, that in good Greek this is called a sow and nothing else.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But a sow of the human kind.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Without question, by Diocles! of my own breed! Well! What think you? will you hear them squeal?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Well, yes, i' faith, I will.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Cry quickly, wee sowlet; squeak up, hussy, or by Hermes! I take you back to the house.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Is that a little sow, or not?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Yes, it seems so; but let it grow up, and it will be a fine fat cunt.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** In five years it will be just like its mother.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But it cannot be sacrificed.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** It has no tail.[88]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Because it is quite young, but in good time it will have a big one, thick and red.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** The two are as like as two peas.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** They are born of the same father and mother; let them be fattened, let them grow their bristles, and they will be the finest sows you can offer to Aphrodité.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But sows are not immolated to Aphrodité.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Not sows to Aphrodité! Why, 'tis the only goddess to whom they are offered! the flesh of my sows will be excellent on the spit.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Can they eat alone? They no longer need their mother!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Certainly not, nor their father.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What do they like most?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Whatever is given them; but ask for yourself.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Speak! little sow.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DAUGHTER** Wee-wee, wee-wee!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Can you eat chick-pease?[89]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DAUGHTER** Wee-wee, wee-wee, wee-wee!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And Attic figs?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DAUGHTER** Wee-wee, wee-wee!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What sharp squeaks at the name of figs. Come, let some figs be brought for these little pigs. Will they eat them? Goodness! how they munch them, what a grinding of teeth, mighty Heracles! I believe those pigs hail from the land of the Voracians. But surely, 'tis impossible they have bolted all the figs!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Yes, certainly, bar this one that I took from them.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! what funny creatures! For what sum will you sell them?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** I will give you one for a bunch of garlic, and the other, if you like, for a quart measure of salt.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I buy them of you. Wait for me here.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** The deal is done. Hermes, god of good traders, grant I may sell both my wife and my mother in the same way!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **AN INFORMER** Hi! fellow, what countryman are you?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** I am a pig-merchant from Megara.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **INFORMER** I shall denounce both your pigs and yourself as public enemies.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Ah! here our troubles begin afresh!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **INFORMER** Let go that sack. I will punish your Megarian lingo.[90]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Dicæopolis, Dicæopolis, they want to denounce me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Who dares do this thing? Inspectors, drive out the Informers. Ah! you offer to enlighten us without a lamp![91]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **INFORMER** What! I may not denounce our enemies?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Have a care for yourself, if you don't go off pretty quick to denounce elsewhere.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** What a plague to Athens!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Be reassured, Megarian. Here is the value of your two swine, the garlic and the salt. Farewell and much happiness!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Ah! we never have that amongst us.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Well! may the inopportune wish apply to myself.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **MEGARIAN** Farewell, dear little sows, and seek, far from your father, to munch your bread with salt, if they give you any.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Here is a man truly happy. See how everything succeeds to his wish. Peacefully seated in his market, he will earn his living; woe to Ctesias,[92] and all other informers, who dare to enter there! You will not be cheated as to the value of wares, you will not again see Prepis[93] wiping his foul rump, nor will Cleonymus[94] jostle you; you will take your walks, clothed in a fine tunic, without meeting Hyperbolus[95] and his unceasing quibblings, without being accosted on the public place by any importunate fellow, neither by Cratinus,[96] shaven in the fashion of the debauchees, nor by this musician, who plagues us with his silly improvisations, Artemo, with his arm-pits stinking as foul as a goat, like his father before him. You will not be the butt of the villainous Pauson's[97] jeers, nor of Lysistratus,[98] the disgrace of the Cholargian deme, who is the incarnation of all the vices, and endures cold and hunger more than thirty days in the month.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **A BŒOTIAN** By Heracles! my shoulder is quite black and blue. Ismenias, put the penny-royal down there very gently, and all of you, musicians from Thebes, pipe with your bone flutes into a dog's rump.[99]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Enough, enough, get you gone. Rascally hornets, away with you! Whence has sprung this accursed swarm of Cheris[100] fellows which comes assailing my door?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** Ah! by Iolas![101] Drive them off, my dear host, you will please me immensely; all the way from Thebes, they were there piping behind me and have completely stripped my penny-royal of its blossom. But will you buy anything of me, some chickens or some locusts?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! good day, Bœotian, eater of good round loaves.[102] What do you bring?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** All that is good in Bœotia, marjoram, penny-royal, rush-mats, lamp-wicks, ducks, jays, woodcocks, waterfowl, wrens, divers.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** 'Tis a very hail of birds that beats down on my market.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** I also bring geese, hares, foxes, moles, hedgehogs, cats, lyres, martins, otters and eels from the Copaic lake.[103]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! my friend, you, who bring me the most delicious of fish, let me salute your eels.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** Come, thou, the eldest of my fifty Copaic virgins, come and complete the joy of our host.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! my well-beloved, thou object of my long regrets, thou art here at last then, thou, after whom the comic poets sigh, thou, who art dear to Morychus.[104] Slaves, hither with the stove and the bellows. Look at this charming eel, that returns to us after six long years of absence.[105] Salute it, my children; as for myself, I will supply coal to do honour to the stranger. Take it into my house; death itself could not separate me from her, if cooked with beet leaves.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** And what will you give me in return?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** It will pay for your market dues. And as to the rest, what do you wish to sell me?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** On what terms? For ready-money or in wares from these parts?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** I would take some Athenian produce, that we have not got in Bœotia.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Phaleric anchovies, pottery?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** Anchovies, pottery? But these we have. I want produce that is wanting with us and that is plentiful here.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! I have the very thing; take away an Informer, packed up carefully as crockery-ware.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** By the twin gods! I should earn big money, if I took one; I would exhibit him as an ape full of spite.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Hah! here we have Nicarchus,[106] who comes to denounce you.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But in his case the whole is one mass of ill-nature.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** Whose are these goods?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Mine; they come from Bœotia, I call Zeus to witness.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** I denounce them as coming from an enemy's country.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** What! you declare war against birds?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** And I am going to denounce you too.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** What harm have I done you?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** I will say it for the benefit of those that listen; you introduce lamp-wicks from an enemy's country.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Then you go as far as denouncing a wick.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** It needs but one to set an arsenal afire.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** A wick set an arsenal ablaze! But how, great gods?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** Should a Bœotian attach it to an insect's wing, and, taking advantage of a violent north wind, throw it by means of a tube into the arsenal and the fire once get hold of the vessels, everything would soon be devoured by the flames.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! wretch! an insect and a wick would devour everything. (*He strikes him.*)
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **NICARCHUS** (*to the Chorus*) You will bear witness, that he mishandles me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Shut his mouth. Give him some hay; I am going to pack him up as a vase, that he may not get broken on the road.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Pack up your goods carefully, friend; that the stranger may not break it when taking it away.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I shall take great care with it, for one would say he is cracked already; he rings with a false note, which the gods abhor.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** But what will be done with him?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** This is a vase good for all purposes; it will be used as a vessel for holding all foul things, a mortar for pounding together law-suits, a lamp for spying upon accounts, and as a cup for the mixing up and poisoning of everything.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** None could ever trust a vessel for domestic use that has such a ring about it.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! it is strong, my friend, and will never get broken, if care is taken to hang it head downwards.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** There! it is well packed now!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** Marry, I will proceed to carry off my bundle.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Farewell, worthiest of strangers, take this Informer, good for anything, and fling him where you like.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Bah! this rogue has given me enough trouble to pack! Here! Bœotian, pick up your pottery.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BŒOTIAN** Stoop, Ismenias, that I may put it on your shoulder, and be very careful with it.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** You carry nothing worth having; however, take it, for you will profit by your bargain; the Informers will bring you luck.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **A SERVANT OF LAMACHUS** Dicæopolis!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What do want crying this gait?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SERVANT** Lamachus wants to keep the Feast of Cups,[107] and I come by his order to bid you one drachma for some thrushes and three more for a Copaic eel.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And who is this Lamachus, who demands an eel?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SERVANT** 'Tis the terrible, indefatigable Lamachus, he, who is always brandishing his fearful Gorgon's head and the three plumes which o'ershadow his helmet.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, no, he will get nothing, even though he gave me his buckler.
