Let him eat salt fish, while he shakes his plumes, and, if he comes here making any din, I shall call the inspectors. As for myself, I shall take away all these goods; I go home on thrushes' wings and blackbirds' pinions.[108]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** You see, citizens, you see the good fortune which this man owes to his prudence, to his profound wisdom. You see how, since he has concluded peace, he buys what is useful in the household and good to eat hot. All good things flow towards him unsought. Never will I welcome the god of war in my house; never shall he chant the 'Harmodius' at my table;[109] he is a sot, who comes feasting with those who are overflowing with good things and brings all sorts of mischief at his heels. He overthrows, ruins, rips open; 'tis vain to make him a thousand offers, "be seated, pray, drink this cup, proffered in all friendship," he burns our vine-stocks and brutally pours out the wine from our vineyards on the ground. This man, on the other hand, covers his table with a thousand dishes; proud of his good fortunes, he has had these feathers cast before his door to show us how he lives.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! Peace! companion of fair Aphrodité and of the sweet Graces, how charming are your features and yet I never knew it! Would that Eros might join me to thee, Eros, crowned with roses as Zeuxis[110] shows him to us! Perhaps I seem somewhat old to you, but I am yet able to make you a threefold offering; despite my age, I could plant a long row of vines for you; then beside these some tender cuttings from the fig; finally a young vine-stock, loaded with fruit and all round the field olive trees, which would furnish us with oil, wherewith to anoint us both at the New Moons.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** List, ye people! As was the custom of your forebears, empty a full pitcher of wine at the call of the trumpet; he, who first sees the bottom, shall get a wine-skin as round and plump as Ctesiphon's belly.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Women, children, have you not heard? Faith! do you not heed the herald? Quick! let the hares boil and roast merrily; keep them a-turning; withdraw them from the flame; prepare the chaplets; reach me the skewers that I may spit the thrushes.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** I envy you your wisdom and even more your good cheer.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What then will you say when you see the thrushes roasting?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Slave! stir up the fire.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** See, how he knows his business, what a perfect cook! How well he understands the way to prepare a good dinner!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **A HUSBANDMAN** Ah! woe is me!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Heracles! What have we here?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** A most miserable man.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Keep your misery for yourself.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** Ah! friend! since you alone are enjoying peace, grant me a part of your truce, were it but five years.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What has happened to you?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** I am ruined; I have lost a pair of steers.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** The Bœotians seized them at Phylé.[111]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! poor wretch! and yet you have not left off white?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** Their dung made my wealth.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What can I do in the matter?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** Crying for my beasts has lost me my eyesight. Ah! if you care for poor Dercetes of Phylé, anoint mine eyes quickly with your balm of peace.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But, my poor fellow, I do not practise medicine.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** Come, I adjure you; perchance I shall recover my steers.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** 'Tis impossible; away, go and whine to the disciples of Pittalus.[112]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** Grant me but one drop of peace; pour it into this reedlet.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** No, not a particle; go a-weeping elsewhere.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HUSBANDMAN** Oh! oh! oh! my poor beasts!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** This man has discovered the sweetest enjoyment in peace; he will share it with none.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Pour honey over this tripe; set it before the fire to dry.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** What lofty tones he uses! Did you hear him?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Get the eels on the gridiron!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** You are killing me with hunger; your smoke is choking your neighbours, and you split our ears with your bawling.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Have this fried and let it be nicely browned.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **A BRIDESMAID** Dicæopolis! Dicæopolis!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BRIDESMAID** A young bridegroom sends you these viands from the marriage feast.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Whoever he be, I thank him.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BRIDESMAID** And in return, he prays you to pour a glass of peace into this vase, that he may not have to go to the front and may stay at home to do his duty to his young wife.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Take back, take back your viands; for a thousand drachmæ I would not give a drop of peace; but who are you, pray?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **BRIDESMAID** I am the bridesmaid; she wants to say something to you from the bride privately.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Come, what do you wish to say? (*The bridesmaid whispers in his ear.*) Ah! what a ridiculous demand! The bride burns with longing to keep by her her husband's weapon. Come! bring hither my truce; to her alone will I give some of it, for she is a woman, and, as such, should not suffer under the war. Here, friend, reach hither your vial. And as to the manner of applying this balm, tell the bride, when a levy of soldiers is made to rub some in bed on her husband, where most needed. There, slave, take away my truce! Now, quick hither with the wine-flagon, that I may fill up the drinking bowls!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** I see a man, striding along apace, with knitted brows; he seems to us the bearer of terrible tidings.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Oh! toils and battles! 'tis Lamachus!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** What noise resounds around my dwelling, where shines the glint of arms.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** The Generals order you forthwith to take your battalions and your plumes, and, despite the snow, to go and guard our borders. They have learnt that a band of Bœotians intend taking advantage of the feast of Cups to invade our country.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Ah! the Generals! they are numerous, but not good for much! It's cruel, not to be able to enjoy the feast!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Oh! warlike host of Lamachus!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Wretch! do you dare to jeer me?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Do you want to fight this four-winged Geryon?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! oh! what fearful tidings!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! ah! I see another herald running up; what news does he bring me?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What is the matter?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **HERALD** Come quickly to the feast and bring your basket and your cup; 'tis the priest of Bacchus who invites you. But hasten, the guests have been waiting for you a long while. All is ready—couches, tables, cushions, chaplets, perfumes, dainties and courtesans to boot; biscuits, cakes, sesamé-bread, tarts, and—lovely dancing women, the sweetest charm of the festivity. But come with all haste.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! hostile gods!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** This is not astounding; you have chosen this huge, great ugly Gorgon's head for your patron. You, shut the door, and let someone get ready the meal.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Slave! slave! my knapsack!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Slave! slave! a basket!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Take salt and thyme, slave, and don't forget the onions.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Get some fish for me; I cannot bear onions.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Slave, wrap me up a little stale salt meat in a fig-leaf.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And for me some good greasy tripe in a fig-leaf; I will have it cooked here.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Bring me the plumes for my helmet.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Bring me wild pigeons and thrushes.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** How white and beautiful are these ostrich feathers!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** How fat and well browned is the flesh of this wood-pigeon!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Bring me the case for my triple plume.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Pass me over that dish of hare.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! the moths have eaten the hair of my crest!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I shall always eat hare before dinner.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Hi! friend! try not to scoff at my armour.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Hi! friend! will you kindly not stare at my thrushes.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Hi! friend! will you kindly not address me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** I do not address you; I am scolding my slave. Shall we wager and submit the matter to Lamachus, which of the two is the best to eat, a locust or a thrush?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** He much prefers the locusts.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Slave, unhook my spear and bring it to me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Slave, slave, take the sausage from the fire and bring it to me.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Come, let me draw my spear from its sheath. Hold it, slave, hold it tight.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And you, slave, grip, grip well hold of the skewer.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Slave, the bracings for my shield.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Pull the loaves out of the oven and bring me these bracings of my stomach.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** My round buckler with the Gorgon's head.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** My round cheese-cake.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** What clumsy wit!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** What delicious cheese-cake!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Pour oil on the buckler. Hah! hah! I can see an old man who will be accused of cowardice.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Pour honey on the cake. Hah! hah! I can see an old man who makes Lamachus of the Gorgon's head weep with rage.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Slave, full war armour.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Slave, my beaker; that is my armour.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** With this I hold my ground with any foe.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And I with this with any tosspot.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Fasten the strappings to the buckler; personally I shall carry the knapsack.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Pack the dinner well into the basket; personally I shall carry the cloak.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Slave, take up the buckler and let's be off. It is snowing! Ah! 'tis a question of facing the winter.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Take up the basket, 'tis a question of getting to the feast.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** We wish you both joy on your journeys, which differ so much. One goes to mount guard and freeze, while the other will drink, crowned with flowers, and then sleep with a young beauty, who will rub his tool for him.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: I say it freely; may Zeus confound Antimachus, the poet-historian, the son of Psacas! When Choregus at the Lenæa, alas! alas! he dismissed me dinnerless. May I see him devouring with his eyes a cuttle-fish, just served, well cooked, hot and properly salted; and the moment that he stretches his hand to help himself, may a dog seize it and run off with it. Such is my first wish. I also hope for him a misfortune at night. That returning all-fevered from horse practice, he may meet an Orestes,[113] mad with drink, who breaks open his head; that wishing to seize a stone, he, in the dark, may pick up a fresh stool, hurl his missile, miss aim and hit Cratinus.[114]
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **SLAVE OF LAMACHUS** Slaves of Lamachus! Water, water in a little pot! Make it warm, get ready cloths, cerate, greasy wool and bandages for his ankle. In leaping a ditch, the master has hurt himself against a stake; he has dislocated and twisted his ankle, broken his head by falling on a stone, while his Gorgon shot far away from his buckler. His mighty braggadocio plume rolled on the ground; at this sight he uttered these doleful words, "Radiant star, I gaze on thee for the last time; my eyes close to all light, I die." Having said this, he falls into the water, gets out again, meets some runaways and pursues the robbers with his spear at their backsides.[115] But here he comes, himself. Get the door open.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! heavens! oh! heavens! What cruel pain! I faint, I tremble! Alas! I die! the foe's lance has struck me! But what would hurt me most would be for Dicæopolis to see me wounded thus and laugh at my ill-fortune.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** (*enters with two courtesans*) Oh! my gods! what bosoms! Hard as a quince! Come, my treasures, give me voluptuous kisses! Glue your lips to mine. Haha! I was the first to empty my cup.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! cruel fate! how I suffer! accursed wounds!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Hah! hah! hail! Knight Lamachus! (*Embraces Lamachus.*)
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** By the hostile gods! (*Bites Dicæopolis.*)
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Ah! great gods!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Why do you embrace me?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And why do you bite me?
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** 'Twas a cruel score I was paying back!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Scores are not evened at the feast of Cups!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** But to-day is not the feast of Pæan.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Oh! support my leg, do; ah! hold it tenderly, my friends!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** And you, my darlings, take hold of my tool both of you!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** This blow with the stone makes me dizzy; my sight grows dim.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** For myself, I want to get to bed; I am bursting with lustfulness, I want to be fucking in the dark.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** Carry me to the surgeon Pittalus.
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Take me to the judges. Where is the king of the feast? The wine-skin is mine!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **LAMACHUS** That spear has pierced my bones; what torture I endure!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** You see this empty cup! I triumph! I triumph!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Old man, I come at your bidding! You triumph! you triumph!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Again I have brimmed my cup with unmixed wine and drained it at a draught!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** You triumph then, brave champion; thine is the wine-skin!
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **DICÆOPOLIS** Follow me, singing "Triumph! Triumph!"
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment

passages.text: **CHORUS** Aye! we will sing of thee, thee and thy sacred wine-skin, and we all, as we follow thee, will repeat in thine honour, "Triumph, Triumph!"
passages.locusKind: Transcription dialogue block, no Greek-verse alignment
